points.title: Saying which person or thing I mean by hanging a clause on it

teach.can_do: I can add a clause after a noun to say exactly which person or thing I mean.
teach.why_it_matters: This is the cheapest complex sentence in English and the safest one to risk. Two short sentences become one, and the reader stops asking which one you meant.
teach.meaning: This kind of clause does one job: it narrows a noun down until only the right thing is left. Say the driver and your listener has a whole depot to choose from. Say the driver who took the Ashfield run and there is one. The clause is not decoration you could lift out. Take it away and the sentence stops identifying anything, which is why nothing is allowed to separate it from its noun.

form.pattern: noun + who / which / that + the rest of the clause
notes: who for people, which for things, and that for either of them in this kind of clause
the relative word stands in for the noun inside the clause, so the noun is never said twice
the verb inside the clause agrees with the noun outside it, however far back that noun is
form.negative: The inside of the clause goes negative in the ordinary way: the driver who does not take the Ashfield run.
form.question: Ask which one? about the noun. Turn the answer into who took it or which arrived late, and hang it straight on the noun.

right.role: the clause that narrows it to one

spec.caption: Nothing comes between the two boxes. No comma, no pause, no breath.

worked_example.sentence: The engineer who checked the Ashfield line has written the report.
worked_example.why_this_form: On its own, the engineer could be any of nine people on that team. The clause cuts nine down to one, and then the sentence can get on with its news.
worked_example.what_the_other_would_mean: Two separate sentences would still be true, but they make the reader hold a person in mind and wait to find out which one was meant.

notice_set.sentence: The drivers who finished the safety course start on the new route in April.
notice_set.question: Do all the drivers start on the new route in April?
notice_set.why: Only the drivers picked out by the extra words start. The others are outside what the sentence is talking about.

notice_set.sentence: The lift that serves the north platform is out of order.
notice_set.question: Can you use a different lift?
notice_set.why: One lift has been picked out. Whether the station has any others is simply left open.

notice_set.sentence: The road that runs along the Verdon floods twice a winter.
notice_set.question: Does the road beside the river flood?
notice_set.why: The added words are how you know which road is meant, and that road is the one beside the river.

notice_set.sentence: Passengers who booked online can board first.
notice_set.question: Can a passenger who paid at the desk board first?
notice_set.why: The permission is attached to one group only, and paying at the desk puts you outside it.

notice_set.sentence: The clinic treats patients who live inside the county.
notice_set.question: Would the clinic treat someone from three counties away?
notice_set.why: Living inside the county is what makes someone one of the patients the sentence means.

teach.rule_line: If taking the words out leaves the reader asking which one, weld them on.
teach.false_rule: That who is for people and that is only for things. That works for people too here, and speakers use it constantly.

errors.wrong: The engineer who I trained him last year has taken over the depot.
errors.right: The engineer who I trained last year has taken over the depot.
errors.why_it_happens: Plenty of languages keep the pronoun inside the clause. The learner builds a complete clause and then adds the relative word in front of it, and nothing feels missing, because nothing is.
errors.smallest_fix: Delete one word: him.
errors.l1_note: Very common for speakers of Arabic, Persian and several South Asian languages.

errors.wrong: The inspector which signed the report has retired.
errors.right: The inspector who signed the report has retired.
errors.why_it_happens: Which arrives first because it is the word learners meet most in written English. The check for whether the noun is a person happens later, once the sentence is already moving.
errors.smallest_fix: Change one word: which becomes who.

errors.wrong: The reports that covers the Sandmouth crossing arrive on Friday.
errors.right: The reports that cover the Sandmouth crossing arrive on Friday.
errors.why_it_happens: The verb inside the clause has to agree with a noun that is now several words behind, and the last thing the learner heard in their head was a singular word.
errors.smallest_fix: Delete one letter: the s on covers.

errors.wrong: The scheme which the council approved in March. It has already run over budget.
errors.right: The scheme which the council approved in March has already run over budget.
errors.why_it_happens: The added clause makes the first group of words long enough to feel like a whole sentence, so a full stop goes in and the real news is left stranded in a new one.
errors.smallest_fix: Delete one full stop and let the sentence carry on.

pays_in.note: Every sentence in a body paragraph that defines who you are talking about.
pays_in.model: The households that struggle most with fuel bills are the ones least able to pay for insulation.

pays_in.note: It is how you identify a person or a place inside a long turn.
pays_in.model: The teacher who taught me to swim was the one everybody at the pool was frightened of.

pays_in.note: Passages define their key terms this way, and the questions test the definition.
pays_in.model: The technique that the survey team adopted had been abandoned almost everywhere else.

used_in.quote: You cannot argue about which services a small town should keep without a sentence that says which services you mean.
The passage introduces its central term and then narrows it with a clause, which is exactly what the first question turns on.

payload.sentence: The trains that stop at Brackenfield are always the slow ones.
payload.question: Is every train on this line slow?

feedback.why_key: Only one group of trains has been picked out, and it is the group that stops at Brackenfield.
feedback.feed_forward: Read the added words as a filter on the noun, not as extra news.

payload.sentence: Staff who work nights are offered a free eye test each year.
payload.question: Does a day-shift nurse get the free eye test?

feedback.why_key: Working nights is what makes someone one of the staff the sentence is about, so the offer stops at the edge of that group.
feedback.feed_forward: Ask who is inside the group before you decide what is being promised.

items.decision_cue: who I interviewed her

payload.context: From a first draft of a report on shift patterns.
payload.sentence: The supervisor who I interviewed her last week runs the whole night team.
reasons: the person is named twice inside the same clause
the wrong relative word has been chosen
the two halves need a comma between them
nothing wrong, it's fine

feedback.why_key: Who already stands in for the supervisor. Her says it again, and the clause ends up with one person too many in it.
feedback.feed_forward: Say the clause on its own and delete anything that repeats the noun.

payload.context: From a paragraph about small towns losing their bus routes.
payload.stem: The residents ___ rely on the last bus have no other way of getting home.

expected: who
that

feedback.why_key: Residents are people, so who is the natural choice, and that is equally at home in this kind of clause.
feedback.feed_forward: Check whether the noun is a person before you reach for which.

payload.context: A student explaining how her course is organised.
payload.stem: The modules that ___ (run) in the evening fill up first.

expected: run

feedback.why_key: The verb inside the clause points back to modules, which is plural, even though evening is the nearest word to it.
feedback.feed_forward: Look back to the noun the clause hangs on, not to the nearest word.

payload.context: Build one sentence about equipment on the Verdon survey.

expected: the sensors that the team installed in march have already failed

feedback.why_key: The clause sits straight after sensors and stops there. The main verb of the sentence is still waiting behind it.
feedback.feed_forward: Put the clause next to its noun, then finish the sentence you started.

payload.given: Some passengers change at Marlow. Those passengers lose forty minutes.
payload.instruction: Write one sentence that says which passengers lose the time.

expected: who change at marlow lose forty minutes
that change at marlow lose forty minutes
changing at marlow lose forty minutes

feedback.why_key: One sentence now does both jobs: it says which passengers are meant and it says what happens to them.
feedback.feed_forward: Fold the second sentence into the noun it describes.

payload.audio_text: The neighbours who've just moved in keep the yard gate open.

expected: the neighbours who've just moved in keep the yard gate open
the neighbours who have just moved in keep the yard gate open
the neighbours whove just moved in keep the yard gate open

feedback.why_key: In speech who've is a single syllable. If you never hear it you will write who just moved in and lose the link.
feedback.feed_forward: Listen for a small extra sound riding on the relative word.

items.decision_cue: which the depot ordered it

payload.sentence: The software which the depot ordered it last spring has never been switched on.

expected: which the depot ordered
that the depot ordered
the depot ordered

feedback.why_key: Which is already the software. Saying it again gives the clause two objects and one of them has to go.
feedback.feed_forward: Delete the pronoun that repeats the noun in front of the clause.

items.decision_cue: that serve the islands

payload.context: Two lines from a timetable notice at Sandmouth.
sentences: The ferries that serve the islands run all winter.
The ferry that serves the islands runs all winter.
meanings: Several boats do this crossing, and none of them stops for the season.
One boat does this crossing, and it does not stop for the season.

feedback.why_key: Both verbs agree with the noun the clause hangs on, so the endings tell you how many boats there are.
feedback.feed_forward: Read the verb endings backwards to the noun to count the things.

payload.prompt_text: A college wants to charge a small fee for evening classes. Write one sentence that says exactly which students would be hit hardest.

feedback.why_key: Naming the group precisely is the whole move here, and it is how a bare opinion becomes an argument a reader can follow.
feedback.feed_forward: Name the group, then narrow it with a clause before the main verb arrives.

payload.prompt_text: Take the body paragraph you wrote on rural services. Rewrite one sentence so that it names the exact group of people affected and finishes with the main point. Two minutes.

feedback.why_key: The commonest way this goes wrong under time pressure is a full stop after the clause, leaving the sentence with nothing to say.
feedback.feed_forward: Check that the sentence still has a main verb after the clause ends.

points.title: Leaving out who, which or that when the clause already has a subject

teach.can_do: I can drop who, which or that when someone else is already doing the verb in the clause.
teach.why_it_matters: It makes your English sound like English rather than like a grammar drill, and it is the shape most people are actually listening for.
teach.meaning: The relative word has a job inside its own clause. Sometimes it is the one doing the verb, and then it cannot leave, because the clause would have nobody in it. Sometimes another subject is already there, doing the verb, and the relative word is only the thing the verb happens to. Then it is carrying no weight, and English quietly drops it. The meaning does not change at all. Only the number of words does.

notes: keep the word when nothing follows it but a verb: the tutor who marked my essay
drop it when a new subject follows: the essay the tutor marked
a preposition left at the end of the clause is normal and stays where it is: the flat we looked at
form.negative: Nothing changes when the clause is negative: the essay the tutor did not mark.
form.question: Put your finger on the word straight after who, which or that. Is it a verb, or is it somebody new?

ends: nobody else in the clause, so the word has to stay
somebody else is already doing the verb, so the word can go

marks.label: the tutor who marked my essay
the bus that goes past the school
the essay that the tutor marked

worked_example.sentence: The form I filled in on Tuesday has gone missing.
worked_example.why_this_form: I is already doing the filling in, so the relative word has nothing left to do in the clause, and English lets it disappear without a trace.
worked_example.what_the_other_would_mean: Putting that back in front of I changes nothing about the meaning. It only slows the sentence down by a syllable and makes it a shade more careful.

notice_set.sentence: The engineer the depot hired last month starts on Monday.
notice_set.question: Who did the hiring?
notice_set.why: The depot sits between the engineer and the verb, which puts the depot in charge of the hiring.

notice_set.sentence: The engineer who hired the new drivers starts on Monday.
notice_set.question: Who did the hiring?
notice_set.why: Nobody else appears before the verb, so the engineer is the one doing it.

notice_set.sentence: The report the council rejected ran to ninety pages.
notice_set.question: Who rejected it?
notice_set.why: The council has slipped straight in after the noun, and that is your signal about who acted.

notice_set.sentence: The tutor I emailed twice has finally replied.
notice_set.question: Who sent the emails?
notice_set.why: I is doing the emailing. The tutor is only on the receiving end of it.

notice_set.sentence: The parcel that arrived this morning is still on the desk.
notice_set.question: Did something arrive this morning?
notice_set.why: Nothing stands between that and arrived, so the parcel itself is what arrived.

teach.rule_line: Look at the word after the relative word. If it is a new subject, you can drop it.
teach.false_rule: That leaving it out is lazy or too informal for an essay. Careful written English drops it exactly as readily as conversation does.

errors.wrong: The bus goes past the school leaves at ten past eight.
errors.right: The bus that goes past the school leaves at ten past eight.
errors.why_it_happens: The learner has stored the rule as the word is optional and applies it everywhere. Nothing in that stored version mentions who is doing the verb, so nothing fires to stop it.
errors.smallest_fix: Insert one word: that.

errors.wrong: The flat we looked at it on Saturday has already gone.
errors.right: The flat we looked at on Saturday has already gone.
errors.why_it_happens: With the relative word gone, the clause looks unfinished, so the learner puts an object back in to repair it. The repair is what creates the error.
errors.smallest_fix: Delete one word: it.
errors.l1_note: Frequent for speakers of Arabic, Persian, Hebrew and several South Asian languages.

errors.wrong: The route the drivers complain about most. It has three level crossings.
errors.right: The route the drivers complain about most has three level crossings.
errors.why_it_happens: With no relative word to signal that the sentence has not finished, the run of words feels complete, a full stop goes in, and the actual news is stranded in the next sentence.
errors.smallest_fix: Delete one full stop and run the two halves together.

pays_in.note: It shortens a clumsy sentence without costing you any complexity.
pays_in.model: The measures governments announce most loudly are rarely the ones that change behaviour.

pays_in.note: Nothing marks the join, so a listener has to hear the second subject.
pays_in.model: The building the college bought last year is still empty.

used_in.quote: Describing a book you recommend needs a run of these: the book I read, the part I liked, the friend I lent it to.

payload.sentence: The tutor my sister recommended has a waiting list until March.
payload.question: Who did the recommending?

feedback.why_key: My sister has arrived before the verb, which means she is the one doing the recommending and the tutor is what she recommended.
feedback.feed_forward: Find the first subject after the noun and give the verb to it.

payload.sentence: The editor who commissioned the piece has since left the paper.
payload.question: Who commissioned the piece?

feedback.why_key: Nothing stands between who and commissioned, so the editor is doing the commissioning rather than receiving it.
feedback.feed_forward: Check whether a new subject appears before the verb.

items.decision_cue: The service runs through Brackenfield

payload.context: From a letter to a local paper.
payload.sentence: The service runs through Brackenfield was cut without any warning.
reasons: nobody else is doing the verb, so the word cannot be dropped
the object of the clause has been repeated
a comma is needed after the noun
nothing wrong, it's fine

feedback.why_key: Runs has no subject of its own here, so the sentence gives the reader two main verbs and no way to sort them out.
feedback.feed_forward: Restore the word whenever a verb follows the noun directly.

payload.context: A tenant writing to a landlord. Put in the missing word only if the sentence needs one.
payload.stem: The damp ___ appeared in the back bedroom has now spread to the hallway.

expected: that
which

feedback.why_key: Appeared has nobody else to belong to, so the word has to stay and hold the clause together.
feedback.feed_forward: Keep the word whenever a verb comes straight after the noun.

payload.given: The college bought a building last year. It is still empty.
payload.instruction: Write one sentence, and leave out the relative word if you are allowed to.

expected: the college bought last year is still empty
that the college bought last year is still empty
which the college bought last year is still empty

feedback.why_key: The college is already doing the buying, so nothing is lost when the relative word goes.
feedback.feed_forward: Drop the word once a second subject is in place.

payload.given: One instrument failed in the first week. That instrument had been borrowed.
payload.instruction: Write one sentence. Decide whether the relative word can go.

expected: that failed in the first week had been borrowed
which failed in the first week had been borrowed

feedback.why_key: The instrument is the thing doing the failing, so there is nobody to take the word's place and it has to stay.
feedback.feed_forward: Ask who fails, who buys, who writes, before you delete anything.

payload.context: Say one sentence about a recipe in your family.

expected: the dish my grandmother taught me takes two days

feedback.why_key: My grandmother slides in straight after dish with nothing to introduce her, and the sentence still finds its main verb at the end.
feedback.feed_forward: Put the second subject next to the noun and keep going.

payload.audio_text: The shift I'd swapped with him fell on the bank holiday.

expected: the shift i'd swapped with him fell on the bank holiday
the shift i had swapped with him fell on the bank holiday
the shift id swapped with him fell on the bank holiday

feedback.why_key: Nothing marks where the clause begins, so the only clue is the new subject arriving with a squashed auxiliary attached to it.
feedback.feed_forward: Listen for a new subject appearing straight after a noun.

items.decision_cue: the guides recommend it

payload.sentence: The path the guides recommend it in summer is closed for repairs.

expected: the guides recommend
that the guides recommend
which the guides recommend

feedback.why_key: The path is already the thing being recommended. Adding it gives the clause a second object and one of them has no home.
feedback.feed_forward: Delete any pronoun that repeats the noun the clause hangs on.

items.decision_cue: the magistrate criticised

payload.context: Two lines from a court report.
sentences: The officers the magistrate criticised have been moved to other duties.
The officers who criticised the magistrate have been moved to other duties.
meanings: The magistrate did the criticising and the officers were on the receiving end.
The officers did the criticising and the magistrate was on the receiving end.

feedback.why_key: The same six words in a different order swap who acted and who was acted on, and only the position of the subject tells you which.
feedback.feed_forward: Locate the subject of the inner verb before you decide who did what.

payload.prompt_text: Think of something you were given as a child and still own. Say one sentence about it, and leave out the relative word.

feedback.why_key: Because someone else did the giving, the relative word is doing no work and the sentence sounds lighter without it.
feedback.feed_forward: Name the thing, add who acted on it, then finish the sentence.

payload.prompt_text: You have one minute on the long-turn card about a book you would recommend. Identify the book, the person who lent it to you and the part you remember, using three of these clauses. Speak it, do not write it.

feedback.why_key: Under real speaking pressure the object slips back in, because the clause feels unfinished without it. That is the habit this turn is hunting.
feedback.feed_forward: Say the clause once, then stop; do not repeat the thing.

points.title: Deciding whether a clause picks something out or just adds news about it

teach.can_do: I can use commas to show whether a clause is telling my reader which one, or telling them something new about it.
teach.why_it_matters: A pair of commas changes how many people you are talking about. Your reader sees what you wrote, not what you meant.
teach.meaning: Both kinds of clause hang on a noun, and there the resemblance ends. One narrows the noun down until the right thing is left. The other assumes you already have the right thing and hands you a fact about it. Commas are the switch between those two jobs, and they are not decoration. Leave them out and you have quietly told your reader that other candidates exist. Put them in and you have said there are none.

form.pattern: noun , + who / which / whose + clause , + the rest of the sentence
notes: that is refused inside the commas; use who for people and which for things
the relative word can never be dropped here, however long the clause is
when the clause runs to the end of the sentence, one comma is enough: we walked to the depot, which shuts at six
form.negative: The inside goes negative as usual: the bridge, which does not carry lorries, reopened in April.
form.question: Before the comma goes in, ask whether your reader could already pick the thing out.

left.role: no commas: the clause says which one
left.text: the drivers who live in Marlow

right.role: commas: you already knew which, so this is news
right.text: the drivers, who live in Marlow,

spec.caption: Same seven words, two different head counts. The punctuation does all of it.

worked_example.sentence: The Sandmouth ferry, which stops running in November, carries about forty cars a trip.
worked_example.why_this_form: There is one ferry at Sandmouth and the reader already has it. The November detail is news about that ferry, not a way of telling it apart from another one.
worked_example.what_the_other_would_mean: Take the commas out and the sentence starts sorting Sandmouth's ferries into ones that stop in November and ones that do not, then picks the first kind.

notice_set.sentence: My aunt, who runs the bakery in Marlow, is retiring in June.
notice_set.question: How many aunts does the speaker have?
notice_set.why: The bakery detail is set apart, so it is not being used to tell one aunt from another. There is nobody to tell her apart from.

notice_set.sentence: My aunt who runs the bakery in Marlow is retiring in June.
notice_set.question: How many aunts does the speaker have?
notice_set.why: The bakery is doing the work of picking one aunt out, and picking out only makes sense when there is a choice.

notice_set.sentence: The two lifts, which were put in during 2019, keep breaking down.
notice_set.question: How many lifts does the building have?
notice_set.why: Nothing is being narrowed down, so the two named at the start are all there are.

notice_set.sentence: The staff, who were told on Friday, have already found other jobs.
notice_set.question: Were all the staff told on Friday?
notice_set.why: Setting the detail apart means the whole group is meant, so the telling reached every one of them.

notice_set.sentence: The staff who were told on Friday have already found other jobs.
notice_set.question: Were all the staff told on Friday?
notice_set.why: One part of the staff is being talked about. What happened to the rest is simply left outside the sentence.

discovery.prompt: Each pair below says something different about how many there are. Work out what is doing that.
pairs: My aunt, who runs the bakery in Marlow, is retiring in June.
My aunt who runs the bakery in Marlow is retiring in June.
The staff, who were told on Friday, have already found other jobs.
The staff who were told on Friday have already found other jobs.
The two lifts, which were put in during 2019, keep breaking down.
The two lifts that were put in during 2019 keep breaking down.

candidate_rules.text: On the left the group is already settled and the clause adds news; on the right the clause is what settles the group.
Commas go in when the noun is a person's relative or a named place.
Use which after a comma and that when there is no comma.

teach.rule_line: Ask whether the reader already knows which one. If they do, the clause takes commas.
teach.false_rule: That the commas are a style choice, or that they mark where you would pause. They mark how many things you are talking about.

contrast.question: Does my reader already know which one I mean?

fork.answer: No, and this clause is how they will find out: no commas
fork.selects: a clause welded straight onto the noun

fork.answer: Yes, it is already settled, and this is news about it: commas both sides
fork.selects: a clause fenced off by commas

a.text: The drivers who live in Marlow have been given parking permits.
a.means: Some drivers live in Marlow and those are the ones with permits. The others got nothing.

b.text: The drivers, who live in Marlow, have been given parking permits.
b.means: Every driver has a permit, and all of them happen to live in Marlow.

contrast.wrong_choice_note: You fenced the clause off with commas. That tells your reader that every driver got a permit and that Marlow is a footnote. If only some of them got one, the commas have just handed over the wrong number.

edge_case.text: In speech there are no commas to see. The difference is carried by a small pause and a drop in the voice, and plenty of fluent speakers do not bother with either. Write them; do not lose sleep over hearing them.

contrast.stronger_test: Put your thumb over the clause. If what is left still names one particular thing, the clause is news and takes commas. If what is left names nothing in particular, the commas would be a lie.

worked_pairs.a: The tenants who complained about the damp have been rehoused.
worked_pairs.b: The tenants, who complained about the damp, have been rehoused.
worked_pairs.gloss: The first says a subset of the tenants moved. The second says all of them did, and mentions the damp on the way past.

worked_pairs.a: The two routes that lose money are being withdrawn.
worked_pairs.b: The two routes, which lose money, are being withdrawn.
worked_pairs.gloss: In the first, losing money is how you know which routes are meant. In the second you already knew, and losing money is the reason being offered.

worked_pairs.a: My cousin who trained as a nurse has moved to Sandmouth.
worked_pairs.b: My cousin, who trained as a nurse, has moved to Sandmouth.
worked_pairs.gloss: The first quietly tells you the speaker has several cousins. The second tells you there is one worth mentioning.

errors.wrong: Students, who fail the January test, must retake the module.
errors.right: Students who fail the January test must retake the module.
errors.why_it_happens: The learner has been told that this kind of clause is extra information, so commas go round every one of them. The commas then quietly claim that the whole year group failed.
errors.smallest_fix: Delete one pair of commas.

errors.wrong: Her sister who works at the clinic has offered to drive us.
errors.right: Her sister, who works at the clinic, has offered to drive us.
errors.why_it_happens: Nobody has ever told the learner that leaving the commas out makes a claim about how many sisters exist. The clause looks like ordinary detail, so it goes in bare.
errors.smallest_fix: Add one pair of commas.

errors.wrong: The Verdon bridge, that reopened in April, is still single-lane.
errors.right: The Verdon bridge, which reopened in April, is still single-lane.
errors.why_it_happens: That is the workhorse relative word and it goes in everywhere by default. Nothing in the way it is usually taught mentions that it will not sit inside a pair of commas.
errors.smallest_fix: Change one word: that becomes which.

errors.wrong: My uncle, lives in Ashfield, has offered us the flat.
errors.right: My uncle, who lives in Ashfield, has offered us the flat.
errors.why_it_happens: The learner knows the relative word can sometimes be dropped and carries that habit across. Inside commas there is nothing else holding the clause to its noun, so the sentence comes apart.
errors.smallest_fix: Insert one word: who.

payload.sentence: My neighbours, who moved here from Ashfield, keep chickens.

feedback.why_key: Nothing is being narrowed down. The Ashfield detail is news about the neighbours the speaker already had in mind.

points.title: Putting the small word in the right place when a clause needs one

teach.can_do: I can keep the small word that a verb needs when the noun it belongs to has moved to the front.
teach.why_it_matters: The preposition carries the meaning here. Drop it and the sentence stops being English; move it wrongly and a spoken answer starts sounding like a legal document.
teach.meaning: Some verbs cannot stand alone: you depend on something, you complain to somebody, you look at a flat. When the thing they need becomes the noun that a clause hangs on, the verb still needs its small word. English gives you two places to put it. It can stay at the end of the clause, where the verb left it, or it can move to the front and take the relative word with it. The choice does not change the meaning at all. It changes how formal the sentence sounds.

form.pattern: noun + (that / who) + subject + verb ... + preposition    |    noun + preposition + which / whom + subject + verb
notes: the everyday shape leaves the preposition at the end: the supplier we ordered from
the formal shape moves it to the front, and then only which and whom will follow it: the supplier from whom we ordered
you cannot move it to the front and also leave it at the end, and you cannot delete it in either shape
form.negative: Negatives change nothing: the supplier we did not order from, the supplier from whom we did not order.
form.question: Say the clause as a plain sentence first. He ordered from them tells you the small word is from.

points.title: Saying how much of a group you mean without starting a new sentence

point_json.grammar_name: Relative clauses after a quantifier: most of which, several of whom

teach.can_do: I can give a total and then say what happened to part of it, inside one sentence.
teach.why_it_matters: This is the structure that turns the commonest punctuation error in academic writing into a complex sentence. One word is the whole difference.
teach.meaning: You often need to say two things about the same group: how many there were, and what happened to some of them. Written English lets you do both in one sentence by hanging the second fact on the first with a quantifier and a relative word. The clause is always news rather than a way of picking the group out, so it is always fenced off by a comma, and the relative word can never be dropped.

form.pattern: noun phrase , + quantifier + of + which / whom + verb ...
notes: which for things, whom for people, and after of there is no third option: that and who are both refused
any quantifier fits in the slot: most, some, several, three, half, none, all, the last of
the same shape works with a noun instead of a quantifier: the cost of which, the results of which
form.negative: None of which and neither of whom carry the negative on their own: the panel heard six witnesses, none of whom were named.
form.question: Ask how many out of how many. The answer is the phrase that goes in front of of.

left.role: two sentences taped together with a comma
left.text: ..., most of them came from one street.

right.text: ..., most of which came from one street.

spec.caption: One word turns a punctuation error into a complex sentence.

worked_example.sentence: The trial produced fourteen readings, three of which had to be discarded.
worked_example.why_this_form: The total and the exception arrive together, so the reader never has to hold two separate facts side by side and work out how they connect.
worked_example.what_the_other_would_mean: Three of them had to be discarded is a second sentence wearing a comma. It says the same thing while telling the reader you cannot hear a sentence boundary.

notice_set.sentence: The department interviewed forty applicants, most of whom had never worked in a laboratory.
notice_set.question: How many of the applicants had laboratory experience?
notice_set.why: Most is counting the ones without experience, which leaves the smaller share on the other side.

notice_set.sentence: The survey used six instruments, two of which failed in the first week.
notice_set.question: How many instruments were still working after that week?
notice_set.why: Six minus the two that failed. The second half of the sentence is arithmetic on the first half.

notice_set.sentence: The scheme, the cost of which has never been published, is now in its fifth year.
notice_set.question: Do we know what the scheme cost?
notice_set.why: The whole point of the fenced-off clause is that the figure has been withheld.

notice_set.why: All of them replied, so the number left over is zero.

teach.rule_line: After of, use which for things and whom for people. Nothing else fits there.
teach.false_rule: That whom is old-fashioned and who will always do instead. After of, who is not available at all.

errors.wrong: The council received two hundred objections, most of them came from one street.
errors.right: The council received two hundred objections, most of which came from one street.
errors.why_it_happens: The second fact clearly belongs with the first, so a full stop feels too heavy and a comma goes in instead. A comma cannot hold two sentences together, and the writer has no other tool to hand.
errors.smallest_fix: Change one word: them becomes which.

errors.wrong: The panel heard six witnesses, two of who were never named.
errors.right: The panel heard six witnesses, two of whom were never named.
errors.why_it_happens: Who is the familiar word and whom feels like decoration, so it gets quietly dropped. After of, English offers no choice at all, whatever the writer thinks of the word.
errors.smallest_fix: Add one letter: the m on the end of who.

errors.wrong: The trial produced fourteen readings, three of that had to be discarded.
errors.right: The trial produced fourteen readings, three of which had to be discarded.
errors.why_it_happens: That is the default relative word everywhere else, so it survives into a slot where it has never been allowed. Nothing in the sentence sounds wrong to the writer's own ear.
errors.smallest_fix: Change one word: that becomes which.

errors.wrong: The clinic wrote to nine families, much of whom replied at once.
errors.right: The clinic wrote to nine families, most of whom replied at once.
errors.why_it_happens: Much is stored as the general word for a large amount, and nobody checks whether the group it points back at can be counted. Families can be counted, so much has nothing to measure.
errors.smallest_fix: Change one word: much becomes most.

points.title: Commenting on the whole thing you just said, without starting again

point_json.grammar_name: Sentential which: a relative clause commenting on a whole clause

teach.can_do: I can add a comment about what I have just said, and make sure my reader knows what the comment is about.
teach.why_it_matters: It is the difference between a sentence that comments on your own point and a sentence that says something about a bridge you never meant to mention.
teach.meaning: Which does not always point at the noun in front of it. It can reach back and take the whole event you have just described, so that the clause comments on what happened rather than on any single thing inside it. Your reader decides which by asking what could plausibly have done what the clause says. When both answers are plausible, the sentence has two meanings, and you will never find out which one your reader took away.

notes: the comment clause always comes last; it cannot be lifted into the middle of the sentence
the comma is compulsory, because without it which fastens straight onto the nearest noun
that is refused here, and so is what, however natural what may feel

points.title: Shrinking a whole clause down to one word and hanging it on the subject

teach.can_do: I can cut a clause down to a single verb form and attach it to the subject of my sentence.
teach.why_it_matters: It is the shortest complex structure in written English and it carries one hidden condition. Get the condition wrong and the sentence says something absurd.
teach.meaning: A participle clause is a clause with the subject and the auxiliary taken out. Living beside the river is a whole clause that has been reduced to two words, and it works because the sentence supplies the missing subject from its own. That is the deal: the clause borrows a subject and the sentence lends it. The -ing shape means the subject is doing it; the -ed shape means the subject is having it done to them.

form.pattern: -ing / -ed clause , + subject + main verb ...    |    noun + -ing / -ed clause + main verb
notes: -ing when the borrowed subject does the action: families living beside the river
-ed when the borrowed subject receives it: samples collected in June
having + past participle when the first action clearly finished before the second: having lost the contract, the firm cut fifteen jobs
when the clause opens the sentence it takes a comma; when it sits behind a noun it takes none
form.negative: Not goes in front: not having heard from the council, the residents wrote again.
form.question: Ask who or what is doing the shortened verb. That answer has to be the subject of the sentence.

errors.wrong: The figures publishing last week show a small rise in rainfall.

points.title: Putting a question inside a sentence without it behaving like a question

point_json.grammar_name: Embedded questions and other noun clauses

teach.can_do: I can drop a question into the middle of a sentence and keep the word order straight.
teach.why_it_matters: It is one of the most visible errors a listener notices, it happens in almost every polite request, and the repair is a single move.
teach.meaning: A clause can do the job of a noun. Instead of naming a thing, it names a piece of information: where the office is, whether the funding will continue, what the council intends. When a question goes into that slot it stops being a question and becomes a thing your sentence is talking about, so it loses the swapped word order that questions carry. The question word stays. The swap goes.

form.pattern: verb / adjective + question word or whether + subject + verb ...
notes: no swapping: where the office is, not where is the office
no do, does or did inside the clause: how much it cost, not how much did it cost
when there is no question word, use whether or if: I am not sure whether it is worth it
the clause can also be the subject of the sentence: what the council intends is anybody's guess
form.negative: The negative sits on the outer sentence or inside the clause, not on both: I do not know why they left.
form.question: Ask what the sentence is about. If the answer is a piece of information, that information is behaving like a noun.

right.role: the same question sitting inside a sentence
right.text: Could you tell me where the ticket office is?

spec.caption: Once the question is inside another sentence, it stops behaving like a question.

worked_example.sentence: Nobody can tell me how long the repairs will take.
worked_example.why_this_form: The question has become the thing the sentence is about, so it sits where a noun would sit and takes ordinary subject-before-verb order.
worked_example.what_the_other_would_mean: How long will the repairs take is a question being asked out loud. Inside this sentence it leaves the reader waiting for a question mark that never comes.

notice_set.sentence: Could you tell me where the ticket office is?
notice_set.question: Is the speaker asking for directions?
notice_set.why: The whole sentence is a request, even though the part about the office has stopped looking like a question.

notice_set.sentence: She asked me whether the office was open on Saturdays.
notice_set.question: Did she already know the answer?
notice_set.why: Asking is what you do when the information is missing, and whether marks the gap as a yes-or-no one.

notice_set.sentence: I can't remember how much the repairs cost.
notice_set.question: Does the speaker know the figure?
notice_set.why: The missing piece of information is the amount, and the sentence is a statement about not having it.

points.title: Splitting a sentence in two so one part cannot be missed

point_json.grammar_name: Cleft sentences: it is X that ... and what ... is

teach.can_do: I can split a sentence so that the part I care about cannot be read past.
teach.why_it_matters: English has almost no way of underlining a word in speech or in an essay. This structure is the way, and it does the job of a raised voice.
teach.meaning: A cleft takes one ordinary sentence and breaks it into two pieces so that one piece stands alone in the light and the rest is pushed into a clause behind it. Nothing new is being said. What changes is which part your reader treats as the news and which part they treat as already agreed. That makes it the tool for correcting an assumption, for setting two things against each other, and for holding the important word back until the end.

form.pattern: It + is / was + the part you want heard + that / who + the rest    |    What + clause + is / was + the part you want heard
notes: the it shape puts the spotlight early: it is the running costs that worry people
the what shape holds it back to the end: what worries people is the running costs
that works for people and things in the it shape; who is available for people
the verb after that agrees with the spotlit part, not with the it at the front
form.negative: The negative usually sits in the spotlight itself: it is not the rent that people object to.
form.question: Ask which single part of your sentence your reader might otherwise skim past. That part goes in the light.

right.role: one part moved into the light
right.text: It is the timing that worries people.

spec.caption: Nothing new has been said. One piece has been moved into the light and everything else into the shade.

worked_example.what_the_other_would_mean: The running costs will decide whether the scheme survives reports the same fact and quietly lets the reader go on assuming the building work matters too.

points.title: Pointing back at something so the reader lands on the right thing

teach.can_do: I can point back at something I have already said and be sure my reader lands on the right thing.
teach.why_it_matters: This is what cohesion actually is. Not linking words, but a chain of pointing that never leaves the reader holding two candidates at once.
teach.meaning: Words like it, they, this and such carry no meaning of their own. They borrow it from something already on the page, and your reader resolves them without noticing, by taking the nearest thing that fits. That is where the risk lives. If two things fit, the reader picks one and never registers that they chose, and you never find out which. A pointing word is only safe when exactly one thing can be at the other end of it.

form.pattern: it / they / this / that / these / such (+ a noun that names what you mean)
notes: it and they point back at a single noun and must match it for number
this and that can point back at a whole idea, which is exactly why they go wrong
the safe habit is this plus a noun that names the idea: this closure, this refusal, this shift
such plus a noun does the same job at a higher register: such measures, such an approach
form.negative: Neither of these worked and none of them was cheap: the negative sits on the pointing word itself.
form.question: Cover everything before the pointing word. Could a stranger say what it means? If not, name it.

left.text: ... and this has never been explained.

right.text: ... and this refusal has never been explained.

spec.caption: One noun after this turns a guess into a fact.

worked_example.sentence: The council shut two of the four recycling points. This closure has doubled the queues at the two left open.
worked_example.why_this_form: Closure names what the second sentence is pointing at, so the reader is never briefly holding two candidates, the council and the shutting.
worked_example.what_the_other_would_mean: A bare this would leave the reader to guess, and a fair share of them would land on the recycling points rather than on the decision.

notice_set.question: What has been criticised?
notice_set.why: Second decision counts along the sentence before it and lands squarely on the route cuts.

teach.rule_line: Every pointing word needs exactly one possible owner. Two owners is a broken sentence.
teach.false_rule: That repeating a noun is clumsy and a pronoun is always tidier. A repeated noun is clear; an unclear pronoun costs far more than the repetition.

errors.wrong: The supplier sent the invoice to the contractor before it had been approved.
errors.right: The supplier sent the invoice to the contractor before the invoice had been approved.
errors.why_it_happens: The writer has one thing in mind and cannot see the other reading at all. The reader has two singular nouns to choose from and takes the nearer one, which is the contractor.

errors.wrong: Schools cut music and drama while protecting sport. This is short-sighted.

errors.smallest_fix: Add one noun after this.

errors.wrong: In the article, it says that fewer teenagers are learning to drive.
errors.right: The article says that fewer teenagers are learning to drive.
errors.why_it_happens: The learner has been taught to open with a phrase and then needs a subject, so it arrives to fill the slot. It now points at nothing, because the only candidate has been shut inside the opening phrase.
errors.smallest_fix: Delete two words: in and it.

errors.why_it_happens: The approaches have already been introduced, so they feel established to the writer. English marks an established thing with the, and without it the reader has nothing telling them to look back.
errors.smallest_fix: Insert one word: the.
